subject: Stanley Kubrick
clues: He refused to fly after a turbulent experience early in his career — he never boarded a plane again.
He spent so long on each film that he would sometimes begin planning the next one during post-production of the current.
He reportedly called Steven Spielberg to apologize after seeing Schindler's List — he had told him he couldn't make it.
He insisted on shooting with natural light where possible, requiring custom lenses developed by NASA.
He adapted Stephen King, Arthur C. Clarke, Anthony Burgess, and Thackeray for the screen.
This American filmmaker directed 2001: A Space Odyssey, A Clockwork Orange, and Eyes Wide Shut.

subject: Apocalypse Now
clues: A typhoon destroyed nearly all the sets, forcing production to pause for months.
The lead actor suffered a real heart attack during filming and continued after partial recovery.
The director funded it partly by mortgaging his own winery and home.
Marlon Brando arrived having not read the source novel — his dialogue was largely improvised on set.
A documentary about its catastrophic production, Hearts of Darkness, became almost as famous as the film.
Francis Ford Coppola directed this 1979 Vietnam War film based on Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness.

subject: Syd Barrett
clues: On his final session with his band, he showed up with his hair shaved and his face coated in Brylcreem and crushed pills.
His bandmates one day simply decided not to pick him up for a gig — and never did again.
He spent his last 30 years as a recluse, returning to his mother's house in Cambridge and painting obsessively.
When he turned up unannounced at the studio while his former band recorded an album about him, no one recognized him.
Shine On You Crazy Diamond was written as a direct tribute to him by his former band.
This British musician was the original creative force behind Pink Floyd before his mental breakdown removed him from it.

subject: Blade Runner
clues: The studio added a voiceover narration and a happy ending against the director's wishes — both were later removed.
The question of whether the protagonist is actually one of the beings he is hunting is never definitively answered.
It lost money on release and was considered a failure — its reputation was built entirely in the years after.
Ridley Scott has given contradictory answers about the film's central mystery in different interviews.
Harrison Ford plays a detective tracking artificial humans called replicants in a rain-soaked future Los Angeles.
Ridley Scott directed this 1982 science fiction film based on a Philip K. Dick novel.

subject: Dostoevsky
clues: He stood before a firing squad — the tsar's pardon arrived only after the mock execution had begun.
He spent four years in a Siberian labor camp, which he later said gave him more than a university education.
A gambling addiction so severe he once lost his wife's wedding ring drove him to write novels under crushing debt deadlines.
He dictated his last novel to a stenographer in part because he could not afford to slow down.
His novels introduced a method of writing in which every character argues a complete worldview — called polyphonic.
This 19th-century Russian novelist wrote Crime and Punishment, The Idiot, and The Brothers Karamazov.

subject: Oum Kalthoum
clues: She memorized the entire Quran as a child and performed recitations publicly before she was ten.
Her concerts in Cairo would stop traffic — not just on the streets, but in cinemas and cafes across the Arab world.
A single song in her repertoire could last six hours in live performance.
When she died, her funeral procession was joined by four million people — more than attended Nasser's.
She performed on the first Thursday of every month for decades — a ritual for the entire Arab world.
This Egyptian singer, known as Kawkab al-Sharq — Star of the East — is the most celebrated Arab musician of all time.

subject: Kafka
clues: He worked as an insurance lawyer by day and wrote only at night, often burning what he produced.
He asked his closest friend to burn all his manuscripts after his death — his friend refused.
He was engaged three times — twice to the same woman — and never married.
His name became an adjective used across languages for a specific kind of institutional nightmare.
He wrote about a man who wakes up transformed into a giant insect, a surveyor who can never reach a castle, and a man arrested without knowing the charge.
This Czech writer authored The Metamorphosis, The Trial, and The Castle.

subject: Twin Peaks: Fire Walk with Me
clues: It was booed at Cannes when it premiered — critics and fans who loved the series called it a betrayal.
Its reputation reversed completely in the decade after release and it is now considered a masterpiece.
It shows the final week of a character whose murder was the mystery driving the TV show it preceded.
Sheryl Lee gave a performance so physically and emotionally demanding it was described as unwatchable on release.
David Bowie appears in a single baffling scene that still has no consensus explanation.
David Lynch directed this 1992 prequel to his cult television series, Twin Peaks.

subject: Jean-Michel Basquiat
clues: He was homeless and selling handmade postcards in SoHo when a collector first paid serious money for his work.
His tag — SAMO© — appeared across lower Manhattan with cryptic phrases like 'SAMO© AS AN ESCAPE GOAT'.
Andy Warhol called him the most talented painter he had ever met — their friendship was misread by critics as exploitation.
He once turned up to a dinner at a collector's house in a paint-covered suit costing $4,000.
He died of a heroin overdose at 27 in 1988, at the height of his market.
This American Neo-expressionist painter went from sleeping rough in New York to selling paintings for millions in under three years.

subject: The Godfather Part II
clues: It runs simultaneously as a prequel and a sequel — two timelines, two protagonists.
Robert De Niro plays the young version of a character Marlon Brando played in the first film.
It is one of the only sequels in history to win the Academy Award for Best Picture.
Al Pacino's performance across the two films charts a man becoming exactly what he swore he never would.
The final shot is a close-up of a face from which all warmth has permanently departed.
Francis Ford Coppola directed this 1974 follow-up, widely considered equal to or greater than the original.

subject: Rashomon
clues: When it was submitted to the Venice Film Festival, the studio that made it was embarrassed and did not attend.
It won the Golden Lion at Venice and the Honorary Oscar — and the studio still didn't understand why.
The same murder is described four times by four different witnesses, each account contradicting the others.
It introduced Western audiences to Japanese cinema and made its director internationally famous overnight.
It introduced a narrative device so distinctive that the word 'Rashomon effect' entered common language.
Akira Kurosawa directed this 1950 Japanese film about the subjectivity of truth.

subject: The Rwandan Genocide
clues: A radio station specifically designed to incite killing broadcast names, locations, and instructions during the killing.
The UN commander on the ground sent a fax to headquarters warning it was coming — the warning was ignored.
Western governments deliberately avoided using the word 'genocide' to avoid the legal obligation to intervene.
800,000 people were killed in approximately 100 days — faster than any mass killing in recorded history.
Churches where people sought refuge became mass murder sites.
In 1994, the Hutu-led government of Rwanda orchestrated a mass killing of the Tutsi population.

subject: Toni Morrison
clues: She wrote her first novel while raising two sons alone, working as an editor at Random House during the day.
As a Random House editor she championed Black writers including Angela Davis and Muhammad Ali.
Her novel about a mother who kills her own child to prevent it from being taken back into slavery divided critics on release.
She was the first Black woman to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.
Her most celebrated novel, Beloved, was inspired by a real historical case from 1856.
This American writer authored Beloved, Song of Solomon, and The Bluest Eye.

subject: Miles Davis: Kind of Blue
clues: It was recorded in two sessions totaling nine hours — the musicians saw most pieces for the first time in the studio.
It abandoned chord-based improvisation for scale-based improvisation — modal jazz — almost overnight.
It has never gone out of print and still sells tens of thousands of copies a year.
A printing error on its liner notes for decades gave the wrong playback speed for two tracks.
Bill Evans' piano introductions on several tracks were composed on the spot from written instructions.
Miles Davis recorded this 1959 album, the best-selling jazz album of all time.

subject: The Truman Show
clues: The script was originally a much darker, paranoid thriller set in New York.
Peter Weir slowed Jim Carrey's instinct to perform — he had to be physically restrained from mugging at the camera.
The island set was a real planned community in Florida called Seaside.
Its central anxiety about living inside a constructed reality became the premise of an entire philosophical movement.
Jim Carrey plays a man who has been the unknowing subject of a live television show since birth.
Peter Weir directed this 1998 film about a man who slowly realizes his entire life is a television program.

subject: Nagib Mahfouz
clues: He wrote in a coffee shop in Cairo every morning for decades — the same table, the same time.
He was stabbed in the neck by an extremist in 1994, partially paralyzing his writing hand.
He continued to dictate work aloud after the attack rendered him unable to hold a pen properly.
He set his most celebrated trilogy in a single Cairo neighborhood across three generations.
He was the first Arabic-language writer to be awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1988.
This Egyptian novelist wrote the Cairo Trilogy and is the towering figure of modern Arabic literature.

subject: Chungking Express
clues: It was shot in five weeks while the director was waiting for the props for his next film to arrive.
Faye Wong's obsession with The Mamas & the Papas' 'California Dreamin'' became the film's sonic signature.
Two separate love stories share no characters and barely share a geography — they're connected by mood alone.
Quentin Tarantino acquired its US distribution rights personally after seeing it at Cannes.
Faye Wong plays a fast food counter girl who breaks into a cop's apartment and redecorates it while he's away.
Wong Kar-wai directed this 1994 Hong Kong film, made almost entirely on location without permits.

subject: The Cuban Missile Crisis
clues: A Soviet submarine officer's refusal to follow orders to launch a nuclear torpedo may have prevented World War III.
A U-2 spy plane was shot down during the standoff — news that nearly collapsed the negotiations.
Both leaders communicated through back-channels because the official channels were too slow and too monitored.
One of Kennedy's key advisers later said the world came closer to nuclear war than any official account admitted.
Thirteen days in October 1962 brought the US and Soviet Union to the brink of nuclear conflict.
This Cold War confrontation over Soviet missiles in Cuba nearly resulted in nuclear war in 1962.

subject: Radiohead: OK Computer
clues: It was recorded in a mansion owned by Jane Seymour — the band lived there for months during production.
Thom Yorke wrote the opening track in the back of a tour bus, overwhelmed by American highways.
Its title was taken from a line spoken by a hitchhiker in a Douglas Adams novel.
It was voted the greatest album of all time by NME in 1997, the year it was released.
It arrived two years after its predecessor and sounded like it had been made on another planet.
Radiohead released this 1997 album, widely considered one of the most important records of the decade.

subject: Abu Simbel
clues: It was relocated entirely — cut into blocks and reassembled 65 meters higher — to save it from a rising reservoir.
The relocation took four years and involved UNESCO, 50 countries, and 2,000 workers.
Twice a year, sunlight penetrates its innermost chamber and illuminates specific statues — an effect the relocation preserved.
It was largely unknown to the outside world until a Swiss explorer stumbled upon it in 1813.
Four enormous statues of Ramesses II sit at its entrance, each over 20 meters tall.
This ancient Egyptian temple complex in Nubia was built by Ramesses II and is one of the most spectacular monuments in the world.

subject: Marlon Brando
clues: He was expelled from school, worked as a ditch-digger, and arrived in New York with $20 before becoming famous.
He kept his Oscar for The Godfather but sent a Native American activist named Sacheen Littlefeather to refuse it on his behalf.
He recorded his lines onto cue cards taped to other actors' faces during Last Tango in Paris.
He became so reclusive in later life that he rarely left his Tahitian island and communicated mainly by phone.
His mumbling, naturalistic performance style changed what film acting was allowed to look like.
This American actor starred in The Godfather, Apocalypse Now, and A Streetcar Named Desire.

subject: Spirited Away
clues: Its director said he made it specifically for the ten-year-old daughters of his friends — not for adults.
He announced his retirement before and after making it — he came back both times.
The bathhouse at its center was inspired by hot spring resorts the director had visited as a child.
It became the highest-grossing film in Japanese history, eventually overtaken only by a later film of his own.
A ten-year-old girl must work in a spirit bathhouse to free her parents, who have been turned into pigs.
Hayao Miyazaki directed this 2001 anime film, which won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature.

subject: Hannibal Lecter
clues: The character was based on a real doctor the author met as a journalist in a Mexican prison in the 1960s.
Anthony Hopkins spent only 16 minutes of screen time in the film that won him Best Actor.
The character's cannibalism was conceived as a metaphor for the consumption of the weak by institutions.
He was voted the greatest villain in film history by the American Film Institute.
Clarice Starling seeks his help to catch a serial killer while he is imprisoned for his own murders.
Anthony Hopkins plays this psychiatrist and cannibal in The Silence of the Lambs.

subject: The Partition of India
clues: A British lawyer named Cyril Radcliffe drew the borders in five weeks, having never visited the country.
He destroyed his papers and left India the day the borders were announced, refusing his fee.
Between 10 and 20 million people were displaced — one of the largest mass migrations in history.
Trains carrying refugees in both directions were ambushed and their passengers massacred.
The borders between India and Pakistan were announced two days after independence — after millions had already moved.
The 1947 division of British India into India and Pakistan triggered one of the bloodiest migrations in human history.

subject: Kendrick Lamar
clues: He grew up in Compton and watched Dr. Dre and Tupac shoot a music video outside his house as a child.
His album To Pimp a Butterfly was recorded in part with live jazz musicians hired to improvise in the studio.
He became the first non-classical, non-jazz musician to win the Pulitzer Prize for Music.
His 2022 Super Bowl halftime show opened with him sitting alone on a throne surrounded by Kendrick Lamars.
His diss track 'Not Like Us' became one of the most commercially successful diss tracks in rap history.
This Compton rapper is widely considered the greatest lyricist of his generation.

subject: Caravaggio
clues: He killed a man in a brawl in Rome and spent the last four years of his life as a fugitive.
He painted directly onto canvas without preparatory sketches — almost unheard of at the time.
He used common prostitutes and street people as models for biblical figures, which scandalized patrons.
His technique of extreme contrast between light and shadow — chiaroscuro — transformed European painting.
He died alone on a beach in Tuscany at 38, possibly from lead poisoning from his own paints.
This Italian Baroque painter created The Calling of Saint Matthew and Judith Beheading Holofernes.

subject: Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind
clues: Charlie Kaufman wrote the script after a friend told him about a woman who had erased her boyfriend from her memory — a concept he invented.
Jim Carrey was cast specifically against type — the director wanted someone the audience wouldn't expect to cry.
Most of the film was shot on location in real houses and trains, not sets.
The film's timeline runs backward through a relationship being erased from a man's mind.
Joel Barish undergoes a procedure to erase his ex-girlfriend Clementine from his memory — and regrets it mid-operation.
Michel Gondry directed this 2004 science fiction romance written by Charlie Kaufman.

subject: El Sistema
clues: It was started with eleven children in a parking garage with $1,200 of government funding.
Its founder believed that giving a child an instrument was a more effective intervention than any social program.
It produced Gustavo Dudamel, who became conductor of the Los Angeles Philharmonic.
It was replicated in over 60 countries after its methods were studied internationally.
It used orchestral training specifically as a tool for pulling Venezuelan children out of poverty.
José Antonio Abreu founded this Venezuelan music education program in 1975, transforming classical music globally.

subject: The Wire
clues: Its creator was a former police reporter and a former teacher — every institution it depicts, he had covered.
Network executives repeatedly tried to cancel it — it survived on critical reputation alone for five seasons.
Each season dismantles a different institution: police, docks, politics, schools, press.
Its drug dealer characters were written with the same moral complexity as its police characters.
David Simon created it as a 'visual novel' about the death of the American city, set in Baltimore.
This HBO series, created by David Simon and aired 2002–2008, is widely called the greatest television drama ever made.

subject: The Hajj
clues: A single pilgrimage site must absorb more people in one week than most countries host in a year.
The circular walk at its center mimics the orbit of electrons around a nucleus — a coincidence that fascinates physicists.
Stampedes have killed hundreds at a single chokepoint in multiple different years.
Every participant wears identical white cloth — the same garment worn in burial.
It is the largest annual human gathering on Earth, drawing over two million Muslims to one city.
This Islamic pilgrimage to Mecca is one of the Five Pillars of Islam and obligatory for every Muslim who is able.
